chapter: Advice to youth and the art of drumming
title: Jo Jones lifting the Basie band; shading drummers and Sonny Payne
summary: DeMichael recalls Jo Jones lifting the band at a Louisville roller rink; Saunders says Basie needs a drummer who can shade.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I heard Jo Jones lift the whole Basie band. This was right before it broke up and he went to the small band. And remnants of the original band, Harry Edison was still with him
Right, right.
Jo and Walter Page.
Right, right. That was a great bass player.
Yeah, they were playing a dance in
Louisville at this roller rink.
Oh, yeah, right, right.
And I don't know what Jo did. I've talked to him about this, but he did something with the bass drum, and -- played it louder or something. And, man, that whole band just went like that.

Right, well, when you talk about drums and things, drum -- Basie is a good example of that. I mean, his style, and he had to have that certain type of a drummer who shades. He shades. He can play, but he's very effective, but he's almost not heard at one time. This type -- and then if he wants to build, he's got the whole world to build on, because he can go to the limits. And so this is why they're so explosive, you would call it.
Yeah. And also, Basie's band, with Freddie Green, and whoever the bass player was.
Right.
They get that ball of sound. And the drummer has to really get in the middle of that ball.
Right, right, and this is the thing --
I never thought Sonny Payne did. I was not --
No, no. Well, he was a trick drummer.
Yeah.
His old man was a trick drummer, Chris
Columbus. But he was more or less a trick drummer and he looked good.
I mean, someone like Gus Johnson.
Right, right. Yeah, but, see, now, he reminds you of Sonny Greer in his day with Duke, with the flash and all of that.
